warmup.q: You join 1,000,000 payments with a 500-row merchants table. Spark's plan shows SortMergeJoin with an Exchange under each side. How many payment rows go through a shuffle?
options: None, because the merchants table is small
Only the payments whose merchant exists
warmup.why: A sort-merge join hash-partitions both sides by the join key, so every payment is written to a shuffle file and fetched by a reduce task. The demo measured 1,001,000 shuffled records: every payment plus every merchant. A broadcast hash join would have moved none of the payments. The size of the merchants table only helps if Spark actually broadcasts it.

sections.h: A shuffle writes every row to a file for the task that owns its key
sections.html:
Lesson 6 (The Spark execution model) stopped at the Exchange, the shuffle that splits a job into stages. This lesson opens it up. It does the job of the first sort in lesson 2's pipeline, bringing equal keys together, across machines, and it is still the most expensive step in most Spark jobs. Take payments.repartition(4, col("merchant_id")): a million payments in four partitions must end up in four new partitions, one per group of merchants.

Every row has to reach the one task that owns its key, and that task runs later, maybe on another machine. Version 1: each map task opens a connection to every reduce task and streams rows to it as it reads them. That breaks twice. The reduce tasks may not be running yet, because they need free slots and their stage starts after this one. And if a reduce task dies halfway, the rows it had received die with it, and every map task has to send them again.

Version 2: write first, fetch later. Each map task works out the target of every row with hash(merchant_id) mod 4, lesson 3's rule. It sorts its output by that target and writes it to its own executor's local disk, in the folder set by spark.local.dir: one data file holding four blocks back to back, plus a small index file with the offsets where the blocks start and end. When every map task is done, each reduce task fetches its block from every map task's data file, from the same machine or over the network. This is Spark's sort-based shuffle.

The Try it shows the files. Four map tasks left four .data files of about 3.4 MB and four .index files of 40 bytes each. 40 bytes is five 8-byte offsets, [0, 856322, 1767340, 2547897, 3421874], so reduce task 1 reads bytes 856,322 to 1,767,340 of each data file.

Now count the cost for M map tasks and R reduce tasks. The map side writes M data files, and the reduce side fetches M x R blocks. Every row is serialized, compressed (spark.shuffle.compress is on by default), written to disk, read back, sent over the network and deserialized. In the demo, a million rows became 13.7 MB of shuffle write, and the reduce side read the same 13.7 MB. With 1,000 map tasks and 1,000 reduce tasks, that's a million blocks to fetch, most of them small.

Shuffle files stay on disk after their stage, until Spark garbage-collects the DataFrame that made them. That's why a failed reduce task only fetches again, and why running the same DataFrame twice can skip its first stage. The cheapest shuffle is still the one you don't run, so most of this lesson is about choosing. First, though, what all those small blocks cost.

try.title: Find the shuffle files on disk
steps: From the labs folder, run ShuffleFilesDemo. It points spark.local.dir at build/l06/local, shuffles a million payments by merchant_id into 4 partitions, and lists what the map tasks left there.
Predict: how many .data files, and how many bytes in each .index file?
Use the offsets to work out how many bytes reduce task 2 fetched from map task 0's file.

code.title: ShuffleFilesDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l07.demo import org.apache.spark.sql.Row import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col import java.io.DataInputStream import java.io.File /** * Shuffles 1,000,000 payments by merchant_id into 4 partitions, then lists the shuffle files the * 4 map tasks left in spark.local.dir and decodes one index file by hand. */ fun main() { val local = File("build/l06/local").apply { deleteRecursively(); mkdirs() } val spark = demoSpark(localDir = local) val log = StageLog(spark) val byMerchant = payments(spark).repartition(4, col("merchant_id")) // the action: every reduce task reads its whole partition and throws the rows away val (_, stages) = log.run { byMerchant.foreachPartition { rows: Iterator<Row> -> rows.forEach { _ -> } } } for (s in stages) { println("stage %d: %d tasks, shuffle write %,d records / %,d bytes, shuffle read %,d bytes".format( s.id, s.tasks, s.recordsWritten, s.bytesWritten, s.bytesRead)) } val files = local.walkTopDown().filter { it.isFile && it.name.startsWith("shuffle_") }.sortedBy { it.name }.toList() println("files in spark.local.dir (blockmgr-.../xx/):") files.filter { !it.name.contains("checksum") }.forEach { println(" %-24s %,10d bytes".format(it.name, it.length())) } // an index file is N + 1 longs: where each reduce partition's block starts in the .data file val index = files.first { it.name.endsWith(".index") } val offsets = DataInputStream(index.inputStream()).use { d -> List((index.length() / 8).toInt()) { d.readLong() } } println("${index.name}: offsets $offsets") println(" so reduce task r fetches bytes offsets[r] until offsets[r + 1] of ${index.name.replace(".index", ".data")}") spark.stop() }

The name shuffle_0_2_0 means shuffle 0, map task 2. Stage 0 wrote exactly one record per payment, and stage 1 read back every byte stage 0 wrote. The last offset in the index equals the data file's size. Spark also writes a small .checksum file per map task, which the demo leaves out of the listing.

sections.h: Many small blocks: push-based shuffle and remote shuffle services
sections.html:
Look again at the M x R blocks. A block's size is a map task's output divided by R, so the more reduce tasks, the smaller every block. LinkedIn measured what that does at scale in its 2020 Magnet paper. Take 150 GB of map output from 1,000 map tasks. With R = 150 each block is about 1,000 KB; with R = 1,500, 100 KB; with R = 15,000, 10 KB. On LinkedIn's clusters the average block was only tens of KB, and billions of them were fetched every day from hard disks, each one a small random read. About 15% of cluster compute time went to tasks waiting for shuffle fetches, and moving 150 GB of 10 KB blocks through one shuffle service took about 4 hours.

Magnet's fix is to merge the blocks before anyone fetches them. Each map task still writes its blocks locally, then pushes them to shuffle services on other machines, which append every block for one reduce partition into one file. A reduce task then reads a few large files sequentially, and the scheduler places it near them. The same 150 GB moved in just over 5 minutes, and LinkedIn's production jobs ran almost 30% faster end to end. Spark 3.2 shipped this as push-based shuffle. It is off by default (spark.shuffle.push.enabled), and Spark's docs say it works only on YARN with the external shuffle service.

That service matters for a second reason. Shuffle files live on the executor's local disk, so when an executor dies, or is removed because the cluster scales down, its shuffle output goes with it and its map tasks run again. The external shuffle service is a long-running process on each machine that serves those files after the executor is gone. Spark on Kubernetes has none yet; its docs list it as future work. Remote shuffle services fill that gap: Apache Celeborn (a top-level Apache project since April 2024, release 0.7.0 in August 2026) and Apache Uniffle keep shuffle data on their own servers, so it outlives every executor. That makes scaling executors up and down, and cheap spot machines that can be taken away, safe for jobs with big shuffles. Alibaba, Shopee and Bilibili run Celeborn in production.

refs.title: Magnet: Push-based Shuffle Service for Large-scale Data Processing (Shen et al., VLDB 2020)
The ASF announces Apache Celeborn as a top-level project

sections.h: Hash, range or round robin decides where each row lands
sections.html:
An Exchange line names its partitioner: the rule that turns a row into a partition number. Spark uses three.

Hash partitioning, hashpartitioning(merchant_id, 4). The partition is the key's hash mod 4, so equal keys meet, on every machine. That's what groupBy, joins and repartition(4, col("merchant_id")) need. The sizes follow the keys: the demo's four partitions got 250,101, 265,871, 228,299 and 255,729 rows. A merchant with a third of all payments would make one partition huge. One key with far more rows than the others is called skew, and lesson 8 deals with it.

Range partitioning, rangepartitioning(amount_cents ASC, 4), used by orderBy. Each partition holds one stretch of keys: amounts 100 to 67,180 in partition 0, 67,181 to 123,255 in partition 1, and so on. Sort each partition, read them in order, and you have the whole table sorted without one task sorting everything. But where should the cuts go? Spark doesn't know how the amounts are spread, so it first runs a separate job that samples the data to choose the boundaries. That's why the demo's orderBy ran 2 jobs.

Round robin, RoundRobinPartitioning(4), used by repartition(4) with no column. Rows are dealt out like cards, exactly 250,000 per partition. Use it to even out lopsided partitions. It puts each key wherever the deal happens to send it.

coalesce(n) is not a shuffle at all. It merges neighbouring partitions where they are: partitions 0 and 1 become one, 2 and 3 another. No row is written to a shuffle file, so it's cheap. It can only lower the count, and the result can be uneven. It also has a trap. coalesce is narrow, so it joins the stage before it (lesson 6). heavy.coalesce(1).write() doesn't run the heavy work in many tasks and then merge: it runs that whole stage as one task. The demo's coalesce(2) ran its stage with 2 tasks instead of 4. When the work before it is heavy, repartition(1) is faster, because the heavy stage keeps its tasks and only the last step runs alone.

You want Use Shuffle
fewer output files after cheap work coalesce(n) none
equal partitions repartition(n) round robin
every row of a key in one partition repartition(n, col(k)) hash
sorted output orderBy(k) range, plus a sampling job

try.title: Five ways to re-cut a million rows
steps: Run PartitioningDemo. For five operations it prints the plan node, the jobs and tasks that ran, and the rows in each output partition.
Before you read the output, predict which operation runs two jobs and which one has no Exchange.
Look at the coalesce(2) line. How many tasks did its stage run, and why does that matter if the work before it were a heavy join?

code.title: PartitioningDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l07.demo import org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset import org.apache.spark.sql.Row import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.max import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.min import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.spark_partition_id /** * Five ways to change the partitions of 1,000,000 payments (4 input partitions). For each one it * prints the plan node that does it, how many jobs ran, and what ended up in each partition. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() val log = StageLog(spark) val p = payments(spark) val cases = listOf<Pair<String, Dataset<Row>>>( "groupBy(merchant_id).count()" to p.groupBy("merchant_id").count(), "orderBy(amount_cents)" to p.orderBy("amount_cents"), "repartition(4)" to p.repartition(4), "repartition(4, merchant_id)" to p.repartition(4, col("merchant_id")), "coalesce(2)" to p.coalesce(2), ) for ((label, df) in cases) { val node = planLines(df, "Exchange", "Coalesce").firstOrNull() ?: "no Exchange" val (jobs, stages) = log.run { df.foreachPartition { rows: Iterator<Row> -> rows.forEach { _ -> } } } val perPartition = df.withColumn("p", spark_partition_id()).groupBy("p").count().orderBy("p").collectAsList() println(label) println(" plan: $node") println(" ran: ${jobs.size} job(s), tasks per stage ${stages.map { it.tasks }}") println(" rows per partition: ${perPartition.map { "%,d".format(it.getLong(1)) }}") if (label.startsWith("orderBy")) { val ranges = df.withColumn("p", spark_partition_id()).groupBy("p") .agg(min("amount_cents"), max("amount_cents")).orderBy("p").collectAsList() println(" amounts per partition: ${ranges.map { "${it.getLong(1)}..${it.getLong(2)}" }}") } } spark.stop() }

The groupBy's output partitions hold merchants, not payments: 500 merchants hashed into 4 groups of 114 to 133. orderBy ran two jobs, and its first job was the sample; the ranges came out balanced by row count, give or take a few thousand rows, because a sample only estimates where the cuts should go. Round robin gave exactly 250,000 rows each. coalesce(2) has no Exchange and a single stage, and that stage ran 2 tasks: the work before it, generating the payments, ran in 2 tasks instead of 4.

sections.h: spark.sql.shuffle.partitions sets how many reduce tasks you get
sections.html:
Every shuffle needs a number of output partitions. For joins and aggregations Spark SQL takes it from spark.sql.shuffle.partitions, and the default is 200, whatever the size of the data.

Too many costs time on small data. The demo sums a million payments per merchant three times. Thanks to the partial sums (lesson 3's combiner), every run shuffles the same 2,000 rows. With 4 shuffle partitions it took 53 ms. With 200, 221 ms. With 2,000, 854 ms. Each reduce task has a fixed cost: the scheduler has to launch it, and it has to fetch one block from every map task even when the block holds a single row. 2,000 reduce tasks times 4 map tasks is 8,000 block reads for 2,000 rows. Even the bytes grow, because every block carries its own compression framing: the same rows took 20,633 bytes in 4 partitions and 116,064 in 2,000.

Too few costs memory on big data. A 500 GB shuffle into 200 partitions gives each reduce task 2.5 GB to sort or hash. That doesn't fit in the memory a task gets, so the task spills: it writes sorted runs to disk and merges them later, or it fails with an out-of-memory error. The same 500 GB in 64 MB partitions would need about 7,800 of them.

The right number depends on the data, and the data changes every night. Adaptive query execution (AQE, lesson 8) solves most of this at run time. After the map stage it knows the real size of every shuffle partition, and it merges small neighbours up to a target of 64 MB (spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes). The demo's last line is 2,000 partitions with AQE on: one reduce task, 65 ms. Spark's SQL tuning page says to set a large enough initial number and let AQE pick the final one. AQE merges partitions; apart from skewed joins (lesson 8), it doesn't split a big one, so start high.

One more effect: when the reduce stage writes files, each task writes its own. A table written straight after a 200-partition shuffle gets up to 200 files per output folder, lesson 4's small-files problem.

try.title: The same groupBy with 4, 200 and 2,000 partitions
steps: Run ShufflePartitionsDemo. It runs one groupBy over a million payments with three settings of spark.sql.shuffle.partitions, then once more with AQE on.
Predict which run is slowest, and how many reduce tasks AQE will keep from 2,000.

code.title: ShufflePartitionsDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l07.demo import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.sum /** * The same groupBy over 1,000,000 payments with spark.sql.shuffle.partitions set to 4, 200 and * 2,000 (AQE off), and then 2,000 with AQE on. Prints the tasks each run needed and its time. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() val log = StageLog(spark) val p = payments(spark).cache() p.count() // read once into memory, so runs compare the shuffle only for ((partitions, aqe) in listOf(4 to false, 200 to false, 2000 to false, 2000 to true)) { spark.conf().set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", partitions.toString()) spark.conf().set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", aqe.toString()) // a new DataFrame for every run: running the same one again would reuse its shuffle files fun totals() = p.groupBy("merchant_id").agg(sum("amount_cents")) totals().collectAsList() // warm-up val times = (1..3).map { val df = totals() val t0 = System.nanoTime() df.collectAsList() (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6 } val (_, stages) = log.run { totals().collectAsList() } println("shuffle.partitions=%-5d AQE %-3s -> tasks per stage %-10s shuffled %,d rows (%,d bytes), best of 3: %4.0f ms".format( partitions, if (aqe) "on" else "off", stages.map { it.tasks }, stages.sumOf { it.recordsWritten }, stages.sumOf { it.bytesWritten }, times.min())) } spark.stop() }

try.expect:
shuffle.partitions=4     AQE off -> tasks per stage [4, 4]     shuffled 2,000 rows (20,633 bytes), best of 3:   53 ms
shuffle.partitions=200   AQE off -> tasks per stage [4, 200]   shuffled 2,000 rows (62,436 bytes), best of 3:  221 ms
shuffle.partitions=2000  AQE off -> tasks per stage [4, 2000]  shuffled 2,000 rows (116,064 bytes), best of 3:  854 ms
shuffle.partitions=2000  AQE on  -> tasks per stage [4, 1]     shuffled 2,000 rows (116,064 bytes), best of 3:   65 ms

The map stage always runs 4 tasks, one per input partition, and always writes 2,000 rows: 500 partial sums from each map task. Only the reduce side changes, and with it the time: 2,000 nearly empty tasks cost most of a second. AQE didn't change what the map side wrote; it changed how many tasks read it. The times depend on your machine and on what else it's doing; the ratio between the lines is what to look at. The demo caches the payments first, so the runs compare the shuffle and not the data generation, and it builds a new DataFrame for each run, because rerunning the same one would reuse its shuffle files.

sections.h: A join needs matching keys in the same task
sections.html:
payments.join(merchants, "merchant_id") has the groupBy problem twice over. Merchant 42's payments sit in every payments partition, and merchant 42's row sits in one merchants partition. Some task has to see both.

Version 1: shuffle both sides. Hash-partition the payments by merchant_id into N partitions, and the merchants the same way into the same N. Merchant 42 lands in the same partition number on both sides, so reduce task k gets every payment and the merchant row for its keys. It then sorts both sides by key and walks through them together, like merging two sorted lists. That's the sort-merge join, Spark's default when both sides are big. It works at any size, because sorting can spill to disk. It costs a shuffle of both sides: in the demo, 1,001,000 rows and 9.4 MB, and 4 stages. The shuffled hash join does the same shuffle, then builds a hash table from the smaller side of each partition instead of sorting; it's faster when that side fits in memory, and the SHUFFLE_HASH hint asks for it.

Version 2: leave the big side where it is. Merchants is 500 rows. The driver collects them and sends a copy to every executor, and each task builds a hash table from merchant_id to merchant. Each payments task streams its rows through its own copy and joins them in place. That's the broadcast hash join: no payment is shuffled, nothing is sorted, and the join runs inside the first stage. The plan shows a BroadcastExchange under a BroadcastHashJoin. In the demo it took about half the time of the sort-merge join, and its only shuffle was the groupBy after the join. The stepper below shows both joins.

Spark broadcasts by itself when its size estimate for one side is below spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, 10 MB by default. The estimate is the weak spot. After a filter, a join or an aggregation, Spark often can't tell how small a table has become, so it plans a sort-merge join for a table that would fit easily. When you know a side is small, say so: payments.join(broadcast(merchants), "merchant_id"), or /*+ BROADCAST(m) */ in SQL. A hint is a request. A left outer join must keep every row on the left, so only the right side can be broadcast, whatever you ask for.

Broadcasting has a ceiling. The table passes through the driver and a copy lands in every executor's memory. Broadcast a 2 GB table to 100 executors and you've moved 200 GB, if the driver survives collecting it. Keep broadcasts to tables of tens of megabytes. AQE can also turn a sort-merge join into a broadcast join at run time, once the shuffle shows that one side is small; the Spark docs note that this is still slower than planning the broadcast from the start.

stepper.title: Sort-merge join, then broadcast hash join
stepper.intro: The same join two ways: move both sides by key, or copy the small side to every task.

try.title: Join a million payments three ways
steps: Run JoinDemo. It joins payments with merchants and sums per merchant name: with the default settings, with broadcasting turned off, with a SHUFFLE_HASH hint, and with a broadcast() hint while broadcasting is still off.
For each case, find the join node and count the Exchange lines before you read the shuffle numbers.
Which case shuffled exactly 1,000,500 more records than the broadcast join, and why that number?

code.title: JoinDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l07.demo import org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset import org.apache.spark.sql.Row import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.broadcast import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.sum /** * Joins 1,000,000 payments with 500 merchants three ways and prints, for each, the join node in * the plan, what the scheduler ran, the shuffle traffic and the time. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() val log = StageLog(spark) val payments = payments(spark) val merchants = merchants(spark) fun query(join: Dataset<Row>) = join.groupBy("merchant_name").agg(sum("amount_cents").alias("total")) val cases = listOf( "broadcast (default, merchants < 10 MB)" to { query(payments.join(merchants, "merchant_id")) }, "sort-merge (broadcasting turned off)" to { spark.conf().set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "-1") query(payments.join(merchants, "merchant_id")) }, "shuffled hash (SHUFFLE_HASH hint)" to { query(payments.join(merchants.hint("shuffle_hash"), "merchant_id")) }, "broadcast hint, threshold still off" to { query(payments.join(broadcast(merchants), "merchant_id")) }, ) for ((label, build) in cases) { // a new DataFrame for every run: running the same one again would reuse its shuffle files build().collectAsList() // warm-up val best = (1..3).minOf { val df = build() val t0 = System.nanoTime() df.collectAsList() (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6 } val df = build() val (jobs, stages) = log.run { df.collectAsList() } println(label) planLines(df, "Join", "Exchange").forEach { println(" $it") } println(" ran: %d job(s), tasks per stage %s, shuffle wrote %,d records (%,d bytes), best of 3: %.0f ms".format( jobs.size, stages.map { it.tasks }, stages.sumOf { it.recordsWritten }, stages.sumOf { it.bytesWritten }, best)) } spark.stop() }

BuildRight means the right side, merchants, became the hash table. The broadcast joins ran an extra job of 2 tasks: that's Spark collecting the merchants to the driver. Their 2,000 shuffled records are the partial sums of the groupBy(merchant_name) after the join (500 names from each of 4 tasks), not the join. The sort-merge and shuffled hash joins wrote all 1,000,000 payments plus 500 merchants to shuffle files. The last case is the fix you'll use in the lab: broadcasting is off, and the broadcast() hint still gets it. Times move between runs; the order of stages in the list can too.

refs.title: Join strategy hints and the broadcast threshold (Spark SQL performance tuning)

video.title: The shuffle, then a sort-merge join and a broadcast join

analogy: Think of matching every employee in a large company with their department's budget code. One way: move every employee to a desk on their department's floor, and send the budget sheets to the same floors, then match them up floor by floor. That is a shuffle and a sort-merge join, and it works however big both lists are, at the cost of moving everyone. The other way: photocopy the two-page budget list, put a copy on every desk, and let each employee look up their own code without moving. That's a broadcast join, and it only makes sense because the list is short. The analogy breaks on the photocopies: in an office they're nearly free, while in Spark the broadcast table passes through one driver and sits in every executor's memory, so photocopying a phone book for every desk can bring the whole office down.
world: Kafka Streams makes you choose between these same two joins, with different names. A KStream-KTable join needs both topics co-partitioned: the same number of partitions and the same key partitioner, so that card 42's events and card 42's table row land on the same instance. That's the sort-merge join's requirement, and when the keys don't match, Kafka Streams adds a repartition topic, which is a shuffle through Kafka. A KStream-GlobalKTable join gives every instance a full copy of the table and needs no co-partitioning: a broadcast join, and just as limited by the table's size. Oracle's planner picks between hash join, sort-merge join and nested loops on the same reasoning, using table statistics. In Spark you'll mostly meet the case where the statistics are missing, and the broadcast() hint is how you supply what you know.
mistake: The common mistake is assuming Spark will broadcast a small table by itself. It decides from a size estimate, and after a filter, an aggregation or a join it often has no good estimate, so it plans a sort-merge join and shuffles the big side every run. The job works and gives the right answer, so the waste goes unnoticed; on a 2 TB payments table it can be most of the runtime. Read the plan: a SortMergeJoin with an Exchange under the big side means the big side moves. If the other side really is small (thousands of rows, a few MB) and will stay small, add broadcast(...). The opposite mistake is broadcasting a table that grows: a dimension that's 5 MB today and 3 GB next year will one day fill the driver's memory.

compare.note: Both plans join the same rows: they're explain() output for JoinDemo's first two queries, trimmed to the join. On the left, each side has its own Exchange and Sort, so the payments are written to shuffle files, fetched and sorted before the join can start, and the join sits in a later stage. On the right, the payments side has no Exchange: the join runs in the same codegen stage *(2) as the scan, and the only thing that moves is the merchants table, as a BroadcastExchange. When you're tuning a join, look first at what sits under the big side.

steps.say: The hourly job joins the last hour's payments (about 40 GB) with active merchants, then sums per category. It takes 25 minutes. Start with the plan, not the code.
steps.code: // 1. what kind of join, and what moves? val merchantsActive = merchants.where(col("status").equalTo("ACTIVE")) val hourly = payments.join(merchantsActive, "merchant_id").groupBy("mcc").agg(sum("amount_cents")) hourly.explain() // SortMergeJoin [merchant_id], [merchant_id], Inner // :- Sort ... +- Exchange hashpartitioning(merchant_id, 200) <- 40 GB of payments shuffled // +- Sort ... +- Exchange hashpartitioning(merchant_id, 200)

steps.say: Check how big the small side really is. Spark's estimate after the filter was over 10 MB, but the data says otherwise.
steps.code: // 2. measure the side you want to broadcast merchantsActive.count() // 48,000 rows // about 60 bytes a row in memory: about 3 MB, well under any sensible broadcast size

steps.say: Tell Spark what you know. The hint makes merchantsActive the build side whatever its estimate says.
steps.code: // 3. broadcast the small side val hourly = payments .join(broadcast(merchantsActive), "merchant_id") // BroadcastHashJoin, no Exchange on payments .groupBy("mcc").agg(sum("amount_cents")) // still one shuffle, of partial sums per mcc

steps.say: Verify with the plan and the numbers. The payments side should have no Exchange, and the shuffle write should drop from about 40 GB to the partial sums: a few hundred categories per map task.

lab.title: Measure the shuffle, then fix a slow join
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail. The test session turns AQE off and sets spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold to -1, so Spark never broadcasts on its own, like a cluster whose size estimates are too high.

Write ShuffleMeter.onTaskEnd: read the task's shuffle write and read metrics and add them to the four counters. The first three tests use it: a narrow query must show zero, a repartition must count every row, and a groupBy must count one partial sum per merchant per map task.

Look at Joins.enrich. It's the slow version: the test shows that it plans a SortMergeJoin. Fix it so the plan is a BroadcastHashJoin with no Exchange at all. Your meter then proves that no payment moved.
Write Layout.fewer, even and byKey. One of them must not shuffle, one must give equal partitions, and one must let a following groupBy(key) run with no extra Exchange.
Run all eight tests until they pass.
hints: taskEnd.taskMetrics() can be null; return early then. shuffleWriteMetrics().bytesWritten() and recordsWritten(), shuffleReadMetrics().totalBytesRead() and recordsRead().
org.apache.spark.sql.functions.broadcast(merchants) marks a DataFrame for broadcasting, whatever the threshold says.

coalesce(n) merges partitions without an Exchange. repartition(n) deals rows out round robin. repartition(n, col(key)) hashes by the key, and a groupBy(key) after it finds its data already partitioned the way it needs.

drill.title: Pick the join and the partitioning
drill.prompt: From memory, write the Kotlin for three jobs: (1) join 2 billion payments with a 3,000-row currency table so that no payment is shuffled; (2) write one day's filtered payments as about 10 files without a shuffle; (3) re-cut a lopsided DataFrame into 64 equal partitions. Then name what explain() shows for each.

answer.html: // 1. broadcast the small side: BroadcastHashJoin + BroadcastExchange, no Exchange on payments val priced = payments.join(broadcast(currencies), "currency") // 2. merge partitions in place: "Coalesce 10", no Exchange (cheap only if the stage before it is cheap) day.where(col("status").equalTo("CAPTURED")).coalesce(10).write().parquet(out) // 3. deal rows out evenly: Exchange RoundRobinPartitioning(64) val even = lopsided.repartition(64)

recap: A shuffle writes, then fetches: each map task writes one data file of N blocks plus an index to local disk, and each reduce task fetches its block from every map task. M x R blocks in all.
Hash partitioning puts equal keys together (groupBy, joins). Range partitioning gives sorted ranges and costs a sampling job (orderBy). Round robin gives equal sizes (repartition(n)).
coalesce(n) merges partitions without a shuffle, but it pulls the whole stage before it down to n tasks.
spark.sql.shuffle.partitions (200 by default) sets the reduce tasks: too many wastes time on small data, too few spills on big data. With AQE on, set it high and let AQE merge.
A sort-merge join shuffles both sides by key. A broadcast hash join copies the small side to every executor and shuffles nothing. Spark broadcasts under 10 MB by estimate; broadcast() forces it.

explain.prompt: A colleague asks why adding broadcast(merchants) to one line cut a job from 25 minutes to 6. Explain what Spark did before and after, in terms of shuffles.
explain.answer: Before, Spark planned a sort-merge join. To bring each payment together with its merchant, it hash-partitioned both tables by merchant_id: every map task wrote all of its payments into shuffle files on local disk, one block per reduce partition, and every reduce task then fetched its block from every map task over the network, sorted what it got and merged it with the merchants. So the whole payments table was serialized, written, sent and sorted once per run. Spark chose that because its size estimate for the filtered merchants table was above the 10 MB broadcast threshold. After the hint, Spark collected the merchants to the driver and sent a copy to every executor, where each task built a hash table and joined its own payments in place. The payments never moved and nothing was sorted, so the join's shuffle disappeared; the only shuffle left is the small one for the aggregation after it. It's safe as long as the merchants table stays small enough to copy to every executor.

deeper.html:
The shuffle in this lesson is a barrier: no reduce task starts before every map task has finished writing. That keeps recovery simple, because a failed reduce task just fetches again, and it gives batch Spark its clean stage boundaries. It also means a stage can't start reducing until its slowest map task is done.

Other designs drop the barrier. Google's BigQuery moved its shuffle to a separate in-memory tier in 2014, spilling to disk only for large volumes. Because the shuffle data lives in that tier and not with the producer, a consumer reads rows as soon as they are produced, and BigQuery picks the number of partitions while the query runs, since a bad choice can make a query orders of magnitude slower. Spark 4.3's Real-time Mode, which the Stream processing track's Spark lesson met, added pipelined shuffles: producer and consumer stages run at the same time and rows flow between them as they are made. Batch Spark still writes every shuffle to disk between stages, which is why the first Try it found shuffle files at all.
